passage_changes.passage: Vice President C. P. Radhakrishnan made the first-ever bilateral visit to Sri Lanka and held talks with President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in Colombo. The visit highlighted several areas where India and Sri Lanka work together. India has been Sri Lanka's largest trade partner and largest source of tourists, and the two countries signed a free trade agreement in 2000. Cooperation also extends to development projects, including the construction of a solar power plant at Sampur in Sri Lanka. Defence ties are expressed through joint exercises between the armed forces, such as SLINEX, MITRA SHAKTI and MILAN. The visit also brought the Overseas Citizen of India scheme into focus. During this period Sri Lanka joined the International Big Cat Alliance. The two neighbours are separated by the Palk Strait, and the uninhabited island of Katchatheevu lies in that strait. Regional forums such as BIMSTEC and SAARC also feature in the India-Sri Lanka relationship. Sri Lanka's President is Anura Kumara Dissanayake, while its Prime Minister is Harini Amarasuriya. Together, trade, development, defence, diaspora and regional cooperation form the main dimensions of the bilateral relationship discussed during the visit.

Left Wing Extremism, commonly known as Naxalism, is a movement that seeks social and political change through revolutionary methods. Its followers aim to overthrow the central government through armed revolution, relying on violence and guerrilla warfare. Their long-term goal is to establish a communist state based on Maoist principles. The movement has been most active in the forested and tribal parts of central and eastern India. The movement's support has deep roots in the lives of tribal communities. Large numbers of tribal people have been displaced as development projects and mining operations expanded into their homelands. Many tribal families also resent laws that limit their access to forest resources. Poverty and a lack of sustainable means of earning a living push many people towards the movement, and a lack of effective governance is also identified as a contributing factor. Any government response therefore has to address the economic and administrative gaps that the movement draws on, alongside security operations. Development work in tribal areas, including basic housing, water and services, is part of this wider approach.

Gujarat has passed the Uniform Civil Code Bill 2026, and with this step it has become the second state to enact a Uniform Civil Code. The idea behind such a code is that the laws on marriage, divorce and inheritance should be the same for all citizens, irrespective of their religious affiliation, instead of being governed by separate religious personal laws. The Gujarat code creates one civil framework for these areas. It places strong emphasis on gender equality and aims to remove discriminatory practices against women. The code also brings in mandatory registration requirements for both marriages and live-in relationships, and it lays down a formal process for separations. Personal laws have long been a sensitive matter in India because many civil laws are closely linked with religious beliefs. For this reason, the code makes room for certain exceptions. Communities whose customary practices and cultural identity need to be preserved are kept outside its scope. Goa has followed a form of common civil code for a long time, and it is often cited as an example of how such a code can work in practice. Uttarakhand, which came before Gujarat, was the first state to adopt such a code after pre-Independence Goa.

The Mahanadi water dispute is a conflict between Odisha and Chhattisgarh over how the river's waters should be shared. Odisha, the downstream state, says that extensive upstream constructions in Chhattisgarh have reduced the water flowing into its territory. In Odisha's view, this decline threatens irrigation, drinking water supply, fisheries and the ecological sustainability of the state. Chhattisgarh, the upstream state, argues that it has a legitimate right to utilise river waters. It points out that it accounts for a larger share of the basin's catchment area. It also says its projects are necessary for regional development and water security. The conflict is most sharp during the non-monsoon season, when water availability downstream becomes critically important. A central obstacle is that the two states have no formal water-sharing agreement between them. The dispute grew more serious after upstream infrastructure work expanded, and Odisha took the matter forward by approaching the highest court of the country. Efforts at negotiation have so far not produced a shared formula. Both states continue to hold firmly to their positions, and the question of how the water should be divided remains open.

The fourteenth Ministerial Conference of the World Trade Organization, known as MC14, was held in Yaoundé, Cameroon. The meeting ended without consensus, leaving several contentious issues unresolved. Members were divided over the moratorium on customs duties on electronic transmissions, and over agriculture and transparency norms. Observers described the deadlock as a reflection of a deep North-South divide. Because no agreement was reached, the pending issues were passed on to the WTO General Council, which meets in Geneva. The WTO is an intergovernmental organisation that manages and encourages international trade. It succeeded the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and was built on the results of the Uruguay Round negotiations. Its member countries work through several bodies, which share the work of running the organisation and handling trade disputes. Trade ministers and senior officials attend its main gatherings, and the organisation maintains strong relations with the United Nations. Trade disputes form a major part of the WTO's work, and the system for resolving them has been under strain. Members have been debating how to restore a binding system with two tiers. They have also discussed a permanent solution for public stockholding for food security, a demand that India and African nations have repeatedly raised. Fisheries subsidies and support for countries losing Least Developed Country status were also on the agenda.

Air quality around the world is often measured by the concentration of fine particulate matter, known as PM2.5. Health agencies set a guideline for the annual average level of these particles, and a global assessment checks how many places meet it. The assessment discussed here is prepared by a technology company that measures air quality and reports the results. Its coverage has grown over time, and the latest edition includes far more countries and cities than the earlier one did. Wider coverage matters because a place without monitors can look clean on paper while its residents breathe polluted air, and an honest comparison needs data from many locations. The findings are sobering. Only a small share of cities met the annual guideline in the latest year, and that share fell from the previous year. Most of the countries and territories assessed did not meet safe air quality standards. Only a handful of places met the guideline, and at least one city recorded very low particle levels, which shows that clean air is still possible.

Katchatheevu is a small island located in the Palk Strait between India and Sri Lanka. The island is uninhabited, yet its ownership remained a point of dispute between the two countries for a long time. Sri Lanka's claim rests on history, since the island was initially ruled by a kingdom of Sri Lanka in the early medieval period. Sri Lanka also argues that a European power which occupied the island for over a century exercised jurisdiction over the islet. India's claim, on the other hand, holds that control of the island later passed to a zamindari, which functioned under a ruling dynasty. Over the years, maritime agreements tried to settle the dispute and strengthen ties. One agreement allowed Indian fishermen continued access to the island, and a later additional agreement prevented both countries from fishing in each other's exclusive economic zones. After the civil war in Sri Lanka ended, tensions rose over Indian fishermen in Sri Lankan waters, leading to arrests, torture allegations and renewed demands over the island.

India has long had a small number of women in its elected bodies. Successive governments have debated reserving seats for women, and a women's reservation bill has been put before Parliament several times since 1996. The law that was finally enacted reserves seats for women in the Lok Sabha and in State Legislative Assemblies, and it also covers the National Capital Territory of Delhi. The reservation is meant to take effect only after a delimitation exercise is carried out and a census is conducted, so its timing depends on those steps. Supporters argue that the measure advances gender equality and brings a wider range of perspectives into decision-making. Critics note that the law does not extend the same reservation to the Rajya Sabha or to State Legislative Councils. Committees on the status of women have examined these questions since the 1970s. Within the seats already set aside for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, a share is meant to go to women from those communities. The reserved seats are also expected to change over time, so that different constituencies are available to women after each redrawing of boundaries.

Counting people has a long history in India, and ancient texts such as the Arthashastra refer to population counts. The modern census was shaped under colonial rule, when national counts were first taken across the country. Early colonial censuses did not all follow the same method. A later one was designed to be synchronous, meaning that it was taken at one time across the whole country. Caste was recorded in colonial counts, and one of them is remembered as the last caste-based census. After Independence, caste data collection was narrowed, and the census recorded information only on Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. Other backward classes were left out of this official count. In recent years, several states have carried out their own surveys of caste. Another census stands out for a different reason. It is the only one in the modern series to show a decline in population across a decade, which makes it a notable point in demographic history. Since Independence, the country has conducted repeated censuses, and each has added to the record of how the population has changed over time. The census remains a comprehensive source of population data for assessing policies and welfare programmes.

In recent years, the number of districts affected by Left Wing Extremism has fallen sharply, and violence has declined in step. Security forces have moved into areas that were once hard to reach. Specialised units operating from bases closer to remote zones have pressed the movement hard, while the state has also tried to close the gap between remote regions and the rest of the country. Connectivity has played a major role. Better road links have reduced the geographical isolation in which insurgents once moved, and expanded mobile networks have helped counter propaganda and bring tribal regions into the digital world. The state has also gone after the money that sustains the movement. Investigation agencies have carried out operations and seized assets, which has disrupted the networks that supply funds from urban areas. The movement also had a parallel system of governance of its own. Administrative efforts have aimed to replace that system with state institutions, including residential schools and programmes for aspirational districts. Coordination between states has been another factor, making it harder for armed cadres to escape across state borders. A surrender and rehabilitation policy has encouraged many members to give up violence and take up a new life, with cash benefits and skill training on offer.

Rural development in India was shaped in the early 1950s by two government efforts, the Community Development Programme and the National Extension Service. Their performance needed a closer look, so the government set up a committee to examine how they were working and to suggest measures for their better functioning. Its most important proposal was a scheme of democratic decentralisation. This scheme later came to be known as Panchayati Raj. The idea was first put into practice in one State before other States followed. Over the following decades, more committees reviewed how these institutions were functioning. Some studied the administrative arrangements behind rural programmes, while others examined whether panchayats should be recognised and protected in the Constitution. Each report reflected a continuing effort to make local governance more effective. Panchayati Raj thus became a subject of national discussion, not just of local administration. A later constitutional amendment gave panchayats a fixed place in the Constitution, turning them from an experiment into a permanent feature of Indian governance. The journey of Panchayati Raj therefore shows how policy ideas, early trials and expert reports together shaped a system of grassroots democracy.

Monetary policy works through a set of instruments that the central bank can adjust to influence borrowing, spending and investment. The most closely watched of these is the Repo Rate, which sets the cost at which banks borrow from the central bank when they face a short-term shortage of cash. The Reverse Repo Rate moves in the other direction, since it is the rate at which the central bank borrows from banks. Changes in these rates affect loan prices across the economy. When rates rise, businesses and households face costlier loans, and demand slows. When rates fall, borrowing becomes cheaper and spending tends to pick up. Central banks, however, do not rely on one tool alone. They also set rules on how much money banks must hold, buy and sell securities in the market, and provide special windows for banks that need overnight funds. Each instrument has a different reach, and some act faster than others. Students often find it useful to group the tools by whether they work through interest rates, through reserves kept by banks, or through the market for government securities. Policymakers combine these tools according to the economic situation, especially when inflation is high or growth is weak. Careful use of the instruments helps keep prices stable while supporting a healthy pace of economic expansion.

Digital trade became one of the most debated areas at the recent WTO Ministerial Conference. For a long time, members had kept a standing commitment that stopped them from taxing electronic transmissions. That commitment ended at the conference because members could not agree to renew it, so the question of taxing digital goods and services is now open. Members remain divided over whether the arrangement should return in some form. The outcome also reflected a deep North-South divide among members on several issues. Some members have chosen a different route. A group of members has advanced talks on a plurilateral agreement on electronic commerce. The proposed agreement focuses on areas such as data flows, digital transactions and consumer protection. These talks have moved forward even though the moratorium itself was not renewed. Digital goods and services cover a broad range of activities. Software, music, films and digital services all fall within the moratorium's coverage. The Appellate Body, which reviews decisions made by dispute panels, has also been part of the wider debate about how the WTO resolves disputes. Dispute settlement reform is one of the agenda items that members could not conclude at the conference.

Nuclear-powered submarines come in several types, and each type is built for a different role. One type carries conventional weapons, another carries guided missiles with conventional warheads, and a third carries ballistic missiles that may be nuclear armed. The third type is typically the largest and most complex of the group. Submarines of this kind are valued for stealth, which comes from low noise, along with extended submerged operations and improved survivability. India's Arihant-class submarines form part of this picture. The specifications of these submarines are classified, so any sketch of them is only an approximation, and readers should treat such drawings with caution. The programme behind these vessels aimed to create an indigenous submarine fleet with outside help. Taken together, these points show how the class fits into India's wider strategic planning. Readers studying this area often connect design features with the role each submarine plays in a country's defence. The booklet describes stealth as a benefit of these vessels, and it lists extended submerged operations and improved survivability alongside it. The class has been described in terms of its power, its launch capacity and its displacement, though some figures are not publicly confirmed. This is why sketches should be read as approximations rather than exact engineering drawings. Students should keep these categories distinct when answering questions on submarines.

Human spaceflight has a history that began in the early 1960s, when a cosmonaut from the Soviet Union became the first person to travel into space. Soon after, Alan Shepard became the first American in space as part of Project Mercury, and a woman later joined the list of people who have flown. Several other countries have since carried out their own human spaceflight efforts. India is preparing its own human spaceflight programme, called Gaganyaan, which will be India's first such programme and a new stage for the country's space work. The programme aims to send a crew into orbit for a short stay and bring them back safely. Its crew will be selected from a group of astronaut designates, and only some of them will fly on the final mission. Training for the crew takes place at a dedicated centre in an Indian city. An application named SAKHI will help the crew by monitoring their health, reminding them of their dietary schedules and keeping them connected with the ground.

facts.title: Legal framework for inter-state waters
facts.summary: Article 262 empowers Parliament to adjudicate inter-state river disputes and allows it to exclude courts' jurisdiction in such matters. The Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 was used for the Mahanadi tribunal, and the River Boards Act, 1956 provides for river boards. Entries 17 and 56 divide powers between the States and the Union, and the Supreme Court cannot question a tribunal's award but can question its working.
facts: Article 262 empowers Parliament to adjudicate disputes relating to inter-state rivers
Article 262 empowers Parliament to adjudicate disputes relating to inter-State rivers
Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 was used to constitute the Mahanadi tribunal
Centre first tries consultation among aggrieved states; if that fails it may constitute a tribunal
River Boards Act, 1956 lets the Centre establish boards for inter-state rivers in consultation with states
A River Board is to meet at least thrice a year and the Prime Minister is its Chairman
No River Board has been created to date
Entry 17 (State List) covers water supplies, irrigation, canals, drainage and embankments
Entry 56 (Union List) empowers the Union to regulate and develop inter-state rivers in public interest
Supreme Court cannot question a tribunal's award or formula but can question its working

facts.title: Committees on Panchayati Raj (1957-1986)
facts.summary: Several committees shaped the idea of Panchayati Raj before it was given constitutional form. The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended democratic decentralisation, and Rajasthan became the first state to establish Panchayati Raj, at Nagaur, on 2 October 1959. Later committees under Ashok Mehta, G.V.K. Rao and L.M. Singhvi reviewed the system: the Ashok Mehta committee recommended a two-tier system, the G.V.K. Rao committee reviewed administrative arrangements for rural development and poverty alleviation programmes, and the Singhvi committee recommended constitutional recognition of panchayats.
facts: The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) examined the Community Development Programme (1952) and the National Extension Service (1953).
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended democratic decentralisation, which came to be known as Panchayati Raj.
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee recommended a three-tier Panchayati Raj system.
Nagaur, Rajasthan, on 2 October 1959 was the first state to establish Panchayati Raj.
Andhra Pradesh followed Rajasthan in adopting the system in 1959.
The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977), appointed by the Janata Government, recommended a two-tier Panchayati Raj system.
The G.V.K. Rao Committee (1985) reviewed administrative arrangements for Rural Development and Poverty Alleviation Programmes.
The L.M. Singhvi Committee (1986), appointed by the Rajiv Gandhi Government, recommended that PRIs be constitutionally recognised, protected and preserved.
B.R. Mehta is known as the Father of Panchayati Raj and the Architect of Panchayati Raj.

facts.title: Elections, reservation, term and oversight
facts.summary: All members of panchayats at each level are elected directly, while chairpersons at the intermediate and district levels are chosen indirectly. The amendment provides for reservation of seats for SCs, STs and women, and sets a five-year term with time limits for fresh elections. A State Election Commission supervises electoral rolls and elections, and a Finance Commission reviews panchayat finances.
facts: Article 243-C: all members of panchayats at village, intermediate and district levels are elected directly.
Chairpersons at intermediate and district levels are elected indirectly, by and from amongst the elected members.
The village-level chairperson is elected in the manner the State Legislature determines.
Article 243-D: seats are reserved for SCs and STs in proportion to their population.
Not less than one-third of total seats, and of chairperson offices, are reserved for women.
Reservation of seats for Scheduled Castes is not applicable to Arunachal Pradesh.
Article 243-E: a panchayat has a five-year term but can be dissolved earlier.
Fresh elections must be completed before expiry of five years, or within six months of dissolution.
Article 243-K: a State Election Commission supervises electoral rolls and the conduct of panchayat elections; its State Election Commissioner is appointed by the Governor.
Article 243-I: the Governor constitutes a Finance Commission every five years to review panchayat finances.

facts.title: Economy and Climate
facts.summary: India slipped from 4th to 6th largest economy in nominal GDP in the IMF's World Economic Outlook 2026, behind the UK and Japan. India withdrew its bid to host COP33, which is scheduled for 2028, and it will halt HFC production clearances after 31 December 2027. Under NDC 3.0, India targets a 47 per cent cut in emission intensity from 2005 levels.
